items.title: Learning to Accumulate Knowledge with Mutual Information
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve their performance by reusing knowledge distilled from past interactions. However, curating new experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows remains challenging. Effective knowledge accumulation should limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure that new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Yet training a curator with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge. Therefore, we propose Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories. We couple feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. Together, these signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge. Standalone success rewards also favor entries that are useful on their own. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0\% and 42.0\% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform the evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/LaoKuiZe/Knowledge-Weaver.

items.title: Links oder rechts – die Entwicklung der Händigkeit und ihre Bedeutung im handchirurgischen Alltag
items.abstract: Abstract: Handedness describes the preference for using one hand over the other in fine and gross motor tasks and represents a key manifestation of functional brain asymmetry. Around 90% of the world's population is right-handed. The development of handedness is based on a complex interplay of genetic, epigenetic, neurobiological, developmental psychological and environmental factors. Prenatal movement patterns allow conclusions to be drawn about future handedness at an early stage. However, genetic influences explain only part of the variance, meaning that polygenic and regulatory mechanisms, as well as perinatal and postnatal influences, contribute significantly to the development and stabilisation of handedness. Handedness has considerable clinical relevance for hand surgery. Injuries to the dominant hand frequently lead to greater subjective limitations, longer rehabilitation and a greater impairment of work capacity and quality of life. At the same time, cortical plasticity offers the possibility for adaptive processes. Taking handedness into account therefore influences the assessment of severity, the choice of treatment strategies, the definition of rehabilitation goals, and the interpretation of patient-reported outcomes. Occupational health aspects are also relevant, as left-handed individuals in right-handed-dominated environments have an increased risk of certain strain and compression syndromes. Furthermore, handedness is relevant not only in patients but also in surgeons, for example with regard to instrumentation, training conditions and bimanual coordination. The aim of this review is to bring together the neurobiological and developmental foundations of handedness and to critically examine their significance for diagnosis, treatment planning, rehabilitation and clinical decision-making processes in hand surgery. An integrative understanding of handedness can help to differentiate treatment strategies more functionally and to optimise them in a patient-centred and scientifically sound manner.

items.title: Listen-to-Reason: Listen with Experts, Retrieve over a Graph, Reason with LLMs
items.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) fuse an audio encoder into a large language model (LLM) through multi-stage training. This coupling means that a new domain or a stronger LLM requires retraining, and their answers cannot be traced to what the model heard: a chain-of-thought is a post-hoc account. We propose Listen-to-Reason (L2R), an interpretable-by-design pipeline that passes audio to the LLM through an explicit, human-readable tree: small heads on frozen expert encoders map each chunk of a clip to semantically meaningful nodes on the tree (for speech, music and environmental sound), and a frozen text-only LLM answers from these nodes and an ASR transcript without hearing the clip. Every answer can therefore be traced to the nodes and transcript it read, and the nodes are causal: replacing the deciding node with a distractor overturns 78% of correct answers on SAKURA. With a 7B reader, L2R outperforms all LALMs we compare against on SAKURA and trails them by 6-12 points on MMAU and MMAR, despite training about 1,400x fewer parameters on orders of magnitude less audio data. However, because any LLM can serve as the reader, we show that a stronger reader narrows this gap without retraining any audio component. A new domain is added with one small head: with five labelled clips per species, it outperforms QLoRA fine-tuning of an LALM on the same clips by 13-26 points.

items.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Generation of Transparent, Open-Source Multiphysics Models of Electrochemical Devices
items.abstract: Multiphysics continuum models are powerful tools for studying electrochemical devices, enabling in silico reactor design and resolution of local pH, potential, and concentration fields that govern device performance but are difficult to measure experimentally. However, constructing such models requires substantial numerical expertise or reliance on proprietary software. Here, we show that frontier large language model agents can remove this implementation burden while keeping the underlying physics under researcher control. Using one-dimensional electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO in a porous gas diffusion electrode as a test case, we develop a machine-readable, human-specified modeling harness containing governing equations, parameters, numerical methods, logical build stages, and human-verifiable checkpoints. From this specification, the agent reproducibly constructs complete multiphysics models in open-source Julia. Independently built models, including fully autonomous agent-built models, agree with an equivalent COMSOL implementation to within 0.7% of the peak CO partial current density, and with one another to within 0.04%. Systematically planted errors demonstrate the importance of explicit specifications for reproducibility and reveal the agent's capabilities and limitations in debugging model physics. This framework establishes a more transparent approach to multiphysics modeling in which physical descriptions and governing equations, rather than specialized code, become the primary inputs for computational model development.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Thematic Analysis Workflow
items.abstract: This repository contains materials accompanying Jafarian (2026), Human-in-the-loop LLM-assisted thematic analysis: a validated, reproducible tutorial for large-scale qualitative research, in press in Behavior Research Methods. The repository provides a reproducible, four-step analytic pipeline, including code for post-level coding, chunked thematic extraction, theme consolidation, and result analysis. Materials include analysis scripts, structured LLM prompts embedded within the code, example outputs, and a sample de-identified dataset. The workflow demonstrates how LLMs can be integrated into qualitative research while maintaining transparency, traceability, and systematic human verification during theme development and consolidation. Final themes are derived through a hybrid process combining machine-assisted organization and clustering with human interpretive review and refinement. The repository is structured to support replication and adaptation of the tutorial pipeline using the provided sample data. Code and materials were developed by Mandana Jafarian. Please cite the associated publication when using or adapting this workflow.

items.title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
items.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

items.title: LOCAA: An Agentic System for Automated Lossy Compressor Tuning
items.abstract: Large-scale scientific simulations generate substantial data volumes, making lossy compression essential for reducing storage and data movement costs. However, users configure compressors through numerical error bounds (EBs) while often evaluating results using quality metrics and end-to-end performance. Because the relationship between an EB and these outcomes varies across datasets and compressors, identifying a suitable configuration typically requires exhaustive search, which can be time-consuming and computationally demanding. We present LOCAA, an Large language model-based scientific lossy compression auto-tuning agent that performs compression-in-the-loop search using tool-integrated execution, compressor-aware guidance, and persistent memory. LOCAA supports user-defined objectives and constraints without requiring a specialized search strategy. We evaluate LOCAA across three scientific applications, five compressors, and three use cases: fixed-ratio compression, compression tuning under multiple quality constraints, and compression tuning under quality and time constraints. For fixed-ratio search across twelve fields from two applications, LOCAA requires 1.98x fewer evaluation trials than binary search and 5.03x fewer than FRaZ on average. For compression ratio maximization under joint Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure constraints across six fields from the Community Earth System Model application, LOCAA reduces the average evaluation trials from 61.5 using binary search to 17, corresponding to a 72.4% reduction. Persistent memory further reduces the average number of trials by 27.9% across multiple timesteps of the same field. These results demonstrate the potential of tool-augmented LLM agents to provide flexible and efficient compressor tuning across diverse scientific data and user-defined objectives.

ROUGE-Precision and BLEU-precision results of the proposed framework has outperformed the response retrieval compared to other retrieval techniques. items.title: Lossy Compressive Text Autoencoders
items.abstract: Our work explores learning a compressed latent representation of text, at the intersection of data compression and representation learning. We propose an autoencoder architecture that performs residual downscaling and upscaling of hidden representations along the time axis, with a residual low-dimension discrete bottleneck. We analyze our approach for different quantization methods, training objectives, and datasets. For different levels of compression, we evaluate the similarity between the original and reconstructed text both at the surface-level (BLEU) and at the semantic-level (LLM-based judge). Additionally, we evaluate our models on downstream question-answering and semantic text similarity benchmarks. Our approach results in compressed representations which are on par with lossless text compression algorithms at 2.24 bits per byte on web text data, while having good reconstruction and downstream task performance.

items.title: Machine Deliberation as an Organisational Resource: Toward a Theory of Cognitive Capacity Governance
items.abstract: Organisations have begun to purchase reasoning the way they long purchased electricity: metered, priced per unit and elastic on demand. Large language models sold through per-token interfaces let a firm dial the depth of machine deliberation applied to any problem, from a shallow single pass to prolonged multi-step reasoning, at a price that scales with depth. Management theory is unprepared for this. Its foundational treatments assume cognition is scarce because human attention is scarce, and its resource theories treat computational capacity as background infrastructure rather than as a governed input to advantage. This conceptual paper introduces the construct of governed cognitive capacity, defined as an organisation's metered stock of machine deliberation together with the routines that shape its demand, allocate its depth and assure its outputs. Drawing from resource orchestration, the attention-based view, bounded rationality and the emerging literatures on delegation to agentic artefacts, six propositions are developed linking capacity governance to value capture, including an inverted-U relation between deliberation depth and net value conditional on output verifiability, an allocation-not-access locus of competitive advantage and a transaction-cost boundary for external agent services. A three-plane governance framework - demand shaping, allocation and assurance - organises the propositions for practice. Contributions to theory, implications for managers and an operationalisation agenda are discussed.

items.title: Managing the Road Network
items.abstract: This chapter discusses how an understanding of human factors can be applied to roadworks, road maintenance, routine inspections, kerbside management and motorway traffic management. All roadworks change the layout of a road; at some stage, there are no familiar drivers or other road users through roadworks. Consequently, the design of any traffic management scheme needs to consider fundamental human factors issues of expectancy, credibility, readability of the road, consistency and comprehension, as well as issues of speed management and the effective use of traffic control devices. An important issue in road management is having adequate maintenance of roadway surfaces, as well as all the other road infrastructure that users rely on, including signs and pavement markings. In order to maintain roads and adjacent infrastructure, routine inspections are usually carried out. The question of inspection personnel having adequate skills is discussed: what skills are needed in order to consider road users’ human factors needs? The final two sections of this chapter discuss kerbside management (the control of parking) and human factors aspects of managing motorway traffic.

items.title: Mapping generative AI governance readiness in Kurdistan Region universities
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by challenging established ideas of plagiarism, authorship, academic integrity, assessment, disclosure, digital literacy, and institutional responsibility. Many universities already have plagiarism or academic-misconduct policies, but these policies may not be sufficient for guiding the educational use of tools such as ChatGPT and other GenAI systems. This study examines public-facing GenAI readiness across a 30-university audit sample in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Using website-based document analysis, it assesses publicly available evidence across 11 dimensions: plagiarism policy, academic integrity guidance, GenAI guidance, acceptable and unacceptable AI use, AI-use disclosure, assessment redesign, student AI literacy, staff guidance, privacy and data protection, institutional governance, and Kurdish/local-language accessibility. The findings show that public-facing GenAI governance remains at an early stage. Most universities were classified as Stage 1, indicating low public visibility or a narrow plagiarism-control orientation. A smaller number showed evidence of broader academic integrity or AI awareness, while only one institution demonstrated a more developed public-facing AI governance position. The weakest areas were AI-use disclosure, acceptable-use guidance, privacy protection, and AI-aware assessment redesign. A purposively selected subset of 10 universities (six public and four private after sector verification; 110 coding decisions) was independently double-coded; initial exact agreement was 95.5% and quadratic weighted kappa was 0.975. The study proposes a preliminary four-stage model of public-facing GenAI readiness – plagiarism control, academic integrity, AI awareness, and AI governance – and an 11-component AI governance checklist for Kurdistan higher education. It argues that universities should move beyond plagiarism control toward transparent, multilingual, locally grounded AI governance that supports academic integrity, responsible learning, assessment fairness, data protection, and student and staff AI literacy.

items.title: Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models Part 1.1: From Hybrid Attention to Hybrid Position
items.abstract: The architectural design of Large Language Models (LLMs) is shifting from traditional full-attention-only models to hybrid models, which combine different attention modules to improve long-context efficiency and performance in length extrapolation and context extension. To explain why hybrid models work and how to design them better, we propose Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models. As Part 1.1 of this series, we begin with hybrids of full attention and either sliding-window attention (SWA) or gated variants of linear attention (LA), represented by GLA and GDN. We first observe a Seesaw Effect in Context Extension: LA hybrids benefit more from long-context continual pretraining, whereas SWA hybrids perform better under length extrapolation. We attribute this behavior to differences in the positional inductive biases induced by these attention mechanisms. We find that SWA hybrids suffer from a Short-Context Learning Trap, Short-Window Weariness, and Long-Window Laziness, and require extended windows to enhance performance in continual long-context pretraining. For LA hybrids, we summarize the Matthew Effect of Hybrid Position Extrapolation and propose Sliding-Window Linear Attention, achieving 16$\times$ training-free length extrapolation while maintaining 100\% accuracy on NIAH-SK1 in 64k context length.

items.title: Meta-analysis of AI posture recognition for work-related musculoskeletal disorders prevention in occupational activities: comparison between untransformed, logit and Freeman-Tukey transformed performance
items.abstract: Introduction The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) posture recognition systems in preventing the occurrence of work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) across all occupational activities, following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Methods During May 2026, six databases were screened without publication date restrictions. Selected studies had to evaluate the performance of a posture recognition system using a machine learning (ML) or deep learning (DL) approach to assess the risk level of WMSD development using at least one of the following metrics: accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, precision, and F1 score. Risk of bias, heterogeneity, sensitivity, publication bias, and certainty of evidence analyses were conducted in the meta-analysis. Logit and Freeman-Tukey transformations were applied to the data before pooling and results were compared to those obtained from the untransformed. A meta-analysis was performed by performance parameter and by transformation. Four subgroup analyses were performed: comparison of AI methods, sensor types, professional activities, and ergonomic tools used, using pairwise mixed-effects meta-regressions. Results Among the 1,071 unique entries, 26 studies were included. The logit transformation most closely approximated a normal distribution for all performance metrics without affecting heterogeneity, which was high (I 2 > 90%) in all analyses. Overall performance ranged from 85 to 95% for the five performance metrics. DL significantly outperformed ML by 4 to 16% for specificity, sensitivity, and accuracy, regardless of the transformation ( p ≤ 0.05). Hybrid solutions demonstrated higher sensitivity and accuracy (> 99%, p < 0.05) with low heterogeneity (I 2 < 30%) regardless of the transformation. Occupational activity had a limited influence on overall performance, and no assessment tool consistently outperformed all others across all five performance parameters. Conclusion In conclusion, the logit transformation consistently improved the statistical properties of the data and AI approach, type of sensors, occupational activity, and ergonomic risk assessment tool all significantly influenced the reported performance metrics. However, findings should be interpreted with caution and prudence is required regarding the deployment of the systems under real-world conditions due to the very low level of evidence. items.title: Methods and Practices Supporting Tacit Knowledge Mobilisation in Continuous Improvement: A Rapid Review
items.abstract: Aim: The aim of this article was to identify current research directions concerning the methods and practices for mobilising tacit knowledge in continuous improvement (CI) processes. Methodology: The article is based on a systematic literature review using the rapid review format. The review was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus and EBSCO databases. A search strategy based on three conceptual blocks related to continuous improvement, tacit knowledge, and methods and practices for mobilising tacit knowledge was employed. A total of 67 articles meeting the criteria were identified. After deduplication and screening, 20 publications qualified for full-text assessment, and 14 papers were included in the final analysis and synthesis. Results: Research has shown that the mobilisation of tacit knowledge in CI is most often understood as a process embedded in work practice and requiring direct engagement with actual work processes. The literature abounds with methods for eliciting tacit knowledge based on observation and action learning, interviews, workshops, and reflective meetings, as well as organizational practices for knowledge transfer and tools for knowledge externalisation and codification. The analysis also highlighted examples of modern digital solutions supporting the externalisation and transfer of tacit knowledge in improvement processes, including elements of artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR). Implications and recommendations: Further research is needed to assess the relative effectiveness of methods for eliciting tacit knowledge and to explore how the AI and VR-based solutions can improve the externalisation of tacit knowledge in organizational practice. Originality/value: This article organizes the fragmented findings from the continuous improvement field related to the mobilisation of tacit knowledge, presenting a synthetic overview of the methods, practices, and boundary conditions for its mobilisation in CI from 2015 to 2025. By synthesizing diverse research perspectives, the article contributes to a better understanding of the mechanisms of tacit knowledge mobilisation, including its elicitation, transfer, externalisation, and codification, in the context of continuous improvement processes.

items.title: MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents
items.abstract: Training and evaluating interactive language agents typically requires rich user interactions, yet collecting human feedback is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulated users offer a scalable alternative, but they must both resemble real user behavior and provide useful learning experiences for agents. In contrast, most agent-training frameworks rely on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs, whose helpfulness can make them overly cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous compared with real users. We introduce MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real user interactions. Empirically, our 9B model achieves a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model. Compared with Claude-Opus-5, the strongest baseline on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena, MIMESIS improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points, respectively. We then freeze the simulator and train an agent by interacting with the frozen simulator using multi-turn reinforcement learning. Across eight environments, training with MIMESIS yields better agent performance than training with GPT-5.5 under all nine unseen user simulators, demonstrating stronger generalization to new user simulators. Moreover, we propose Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), which leverages simulator-generated private reasoning traces and subsequent utterances as feedback on how well the agent addresses user needs. A coach converts this information into concise coaching notes that describe how the agent can better anticipate user needs and adapt its behavior over the course of an interaction. CSD turns this feedback into dense, token-level supervision beyond sparse task rewards, yielding further gains across all nine evaluation user models.

items.title: MIRROR: From Imitation to Internalization in LLM Personalization
items.abstract: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.

items.title: Mitigating Bias and Manipulation in DanceSport and Other Judged Sports: A Scoping Review of Training, Governance, Technology, and Data Analytics
items.abstract: FAIR-DANCE is a scoping review of judging integrity in DanceSport and other judged sports. This OSF project hosts the protocol, search documentation, screening and retrieval records, final data-charting dataset, supplementary materials, reporting checklists, and methodological amendment history. The review maps evidence on judging reliability and agreement, scoring accuracy and validity, contextual bias, anomalous scoring behaviour, manipulation and integrity threats, judge education and calibration, competition monitoring and governance, digital systems, statistical analytics, and artificial intelligence-supported evaluation, with particular emphasis on the potential transferability of identified practices to DanceSport. The review was conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute methodological guidance for scoping reviews and is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Search documentation is maintained in accordance with PRISMA-S principles. The original database searches identified 466 records. Following independent screening, charting, and second-check reconciliation, the original analytic corpus comprised 113 studies. A targeted supplementary Scopus sensitivity search conducted on 6 October 2026 identified 10 additional eligible studies, yielding a final analytic corpus of 123 studies. The final synthesis is organised around the FAIR-DANCE framework, comprising Measurement Quality, Contextual Fairness, Integrity Surveillance, Technology Assurance, and Procedural Governance, with continuous judge education and calibration and human-in-the-loop technology as cross-cutting principles. Post-registration methodological amendments, supplementary-search decisions, and the full reproducibility audit trail are documented transparently in this project.

items.title: Model-based visual cue design for mitigating motion sickness: development, theoretical analysis, and experimental validation
items.abstract: Autonomous vehicles are expected to exacerbate motion sickness (MS), since occupants may engage more in non-driving-related activities. Due to their availability and user experience, presenting visual cues of vehicle motion has become an effective MS mitigation approach. However, approaches to designing visual cues rely on empirical methodology and subjective feedback, while overlooking the mechanism link between cue design and MS mitigation effects. Considering both user-friendliness and systematic optimisation, a model-based visual cue design framework is proposed, adopting a computational model capable of quantifying and interpreting the effectiveness of visual cues on MS. Taking a dot-matrix visual cue as an example, driving simulator experiments were conducted, showing that the design framework provides objective and model-informed insights for cue evaluation and refinement. This research may work as a foundation for data-driven design of MS mitigation strategies in autonomous vehicles.

items.title: MorphCL: Morphological Contrastive Learning for Inertial-based Human Activity Recognition
items.abstract: Despite the ubiquity of sensors in wearable and mobile devices and the abundance of human movement data they generate, translating unlabeled recordings into foundational motion models remains an open challenge. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has alleviated the need for costly annotations, yet existing approaches leave the global structure of large-scale motion data largely untapped, relying on randomly sampled batches and local comparisons that become particularly problematic for in-the-wild inertial data dominated by stationary, low-variance behaviors. Here we introduce Morphological Contrastive Learning (MorphCL), a self-supervised pretraining framework that uses structure-aware grouping to inject explicit modeling of global structure into inertial-based SSL approaches. Building on two well-established pillars of motion analysis, the discovery of motion primitives, or motifs, and domain-specific feature descriptors, we show that MorphCL substantially improves linear probing and finetuning results of learned encoders by up to 15 percentage points in F1-score. In a comparison with existing foundation models, we demonstrate that MorphCL-pretrained encoders match or surpass them models in linear probing performance while trained on $4600\times$ less data. Qualitative analysis of the resulting embedding spaces further reveals morphologically meaningful cluster structure, with improved separation of kinematically similar activity classes.

items.title: MotherTree: Meta-learning on synthetic data improves decision tree training
items.abstract: Conventional decision tree algorithms produce effective, transparent models that can be audited, communicated, and deployed independently of the training data, but require learning every new task from scratch. In contrast, tabular foundation models demonstrate that meta-learning from a synthetic prior distribution enables strong in-context prediction for previously unseen tasks, especially in small-sample regimes. However, this approach does not produce a standalone model that can be inspected in isolation. We introduce MotherTree, a tabular transformer that meta-learns decision tree induction: given a training set for a new task, it outputs a hard, axis-aligned decision tree, equivalent in form to classically trained trees, in a single forward pass. MotherTree is pre-trained on a synthetic prior using stochastic gradient descent without requiring reference trees for supervision. On established benchmarks with controlled sample size, the approach is competitive with size-matched trees from common algorithms: recursive partitioning, gradient-based tree learning, globally optimal trees, and distillation from tabular foundation models. Notably, MotherTree consistently improves over from-scratch gradient-based learning and acts as a strong initializer: task-specific tuning of the generated tree outperforms the corresponding from-scratch learner on all benchmarks and sample sizes. These results show that meta-learning can provide effective inductive biases for learning stand-alone, small decision tree classifiers.

items.title: Motivación y elección profesional en estudiantes universitarios desde la teoría de la autodeterminación
items.abstract: Background: Motivation is one of the factors that influences not only the choice of a career path but also the ability to remain in it despite social, economic, academic, or personal difficulties. Objective: To understand the underlying motivations in career choice through Self-Determination Theory (SDT) proposed by Deci and Ryan. Methodology: The research approach was qualitative with a phenomenological design. The unit of analysis consisted of 11 students selected through purposive sampling. The data collection technique was in-depth, semi-structured interviews. Results: The findings reveal the prevalence of intrinsic motivation. Regarding the basic psychological needs of competence and relatedness, there is a positive appreciation for becoming better psychology professionals. Conclusion: Motivation for career choice strengthens over time within a process of meaning-making guided by SDT, which not only sustains academic interest but also fosters a commitment to the quality of the future professional.

items.title: Multimodal LLMs Can Learn to Read Brain Signals: A Vision--Language Model for Unified Multi-Task EEG Decoding
items.abstract: Learning EEG representations that generalize across cognitive tasks, subjects, and recording conditions remains a key challenge in electroencephalography (EEG) decoding. Recent advances in foundation models have improved EEG decoding performance, yet a fundamental open question remains: how to effectively interface neural signals with these models to enable multi-task learning across datasets. To investigate this question, we introduce BraVista, a visual-language framework that encodes multichannel EEG signals as structured images and enables multi-task learning through instruction-conditioned vision-language models (VLMs). Our approach relies on continued post-training of a general-domain VLM, leveraging its visual and linguistic priors to adapt to neural signals without a separate large-scale EEG-specific pretraining stage. We evaluate BraVista on four datasets spanning sleep staging, emotion recognition, cognitive workload classification, and abnormal EEG detection, showing strong performance across these tasks. Further analyses show that the choice of EEG-to-image representation is critical to performance. Moreover, through controlled perturbations of the EEG signal, we observe a gradual performance degradation under increasing noise, suggesting that the model relies on EEG-relevant information rather than superficial visual patterns. Together, these findings establish structured visual representations as an effective and scalable interface between neural signals and general-domain foundation models for unified multi-task EEG decoding.

items.title: Musculoskeletal symptoms and biopsychosocial factors among nursing students: implications for protecting the future health workforce
items.abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders are an important occupational health concern among healthcare professionals and may emerge before entry into the workforce. Identifying musculoskeletal symptoms and their biopsychosocial correlates among nursing students may provide opportunities for early prevention and health promotion. Objective This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of musculoskeletal symptoms and identify associated biopsychosocial factors among nursing students in Türkiye. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 213 nursing students (77% female) in Türkiye. Data were collected through an online survey between February and April 2022. Musculoskeletal symptoms, physical activity, perceived stress, biopsychosocial wellbeing, and coping behaviors were assessed using validated instruments. Associations were examined using chi-square tests and independent-samples t -tests; logistic regression analyses, using a simplified set of six predictors (age, BMI, gender, physical activity, total perceived stress, and total biopsychosocial response score) and Firth's penalized-likelihood method, were performed to identify factors associated with musculoskeletal symptoms. Results Overall, 62% of nursing students reported musculoskeletal symptoms during the previous 12 months. The most frequently reported symptoms were in the upper back (41%), followed by the low back and neck (33% each). High physical activity showed a significant association with lower odds of upper back symptoms (OR = 0.19, p = 0.047) and a borderline association with lower odds of any 12-month musculoskeletal symptom (OR = 0.25, p = 0.060). Female students had higher odds of neck, shoulder, and upper back symptoms than male students (OR = 0.05–0.19 for male vs. female). No stress or biopsychosocial measure was significantly associated with any 12-month musculoskeletal outcome; findings for the hip/thigh region should be considered exploratory given a low events-per-variable ratio. Conclusions Musculoskeletal symptoms were highly prevalent among nursing students, highlighting the importance of addressing musculoskeletal health before entry into the nursing workforce. The findings suggest that physical factors may be more relevant to symptom occurrence than stress or biopsychosocial wellbeing in this sample. Although a biopsychosocial framework provides a useful perspective for understanding musculoskeletal health, further longitudinal research is needed to clarify the role of stress and wellbeing and to inform targeted interventions.

items.title: Navigating the Digital Transformation of Islamic Education: Authority, Verification, and the Problem of Unsourced Religious Content
items.abstract: Digital platforms have become a primary route through which Indonesian students encounter religious knowledge, and teachers of Islamic education increasingly meet classroom questions whose answers students have already obtained from sources carrying no chain of transmission. This study examines how the digital transformation of Islamic education reconfigures the relationship between teacher, text, and learner, and asks what verification practice becomes possible when the volume of accessible religious content exceeds any teacher’s capacity to authenticate it. The study is a conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and institutional reports, selected purposively and analysed thematically across accessibility, content authenticity, pedagogical innovation, teacher role, ethics, and institutional readiness. The analysis finds that digitalisation expands access decisively but redistributes interpretive authority in ways existing teacher preparation does not address; that content generated by artificial intelligence intensifies rather than creates this problem, since fluency without sanad is already characteristic of much online religious material; and that blended learning models developed for school-age learners transfer poorly to the adult and para-professional audiences that dominate Islamic non-formal education without andragogical adjustment. The study argues that the practical task facing institutions is not the adoption of technology but the design of verification competence, and proposes three design principles: teaching provenance rather than conclusions, making the limits of teacher authority explicit, and building institutional review of digital content into curriculum governance rather than leaving it to individual discretion.

items.title: Neuraxial Medication Administration Errors During Anaesthesia and Perioperative Management, Consequences, Contributing Human and Systemic Factors and Their Prevention: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: This systematic review aimed to investigate neuraxial administration errors, examine their contributing factors, and evaluate clinical outcomes using a novel harm scale. METHODS: The author searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar for reports from 1981 to 2025 in any language. Exclusions were reviews, overdose incidents, and non-neuraxial administrations. Harm was classified using a novel five-level scale, and contributing factors were identified using the Human and Systemic Factors Analysis Classification System (HFACS). RESULTS: The search revealed 50 reports (54 patients), mainly involving the epidural route (38 vs 16 intrathecal), non-obstetric patients (35 vs 17 obstetric), and female gender (73%). Medications were grouped into nine divisions: IV fluids/total parenteral nutrition/insulin, anticholinergics, antiseptics, antiemetics, anticoagulants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, opioids, Syntocinon, and others. Atropine (6 patients) was the most common, followed by remifentanil (4), Syntocinon (4), chlorhexidine (3), and water (3). Level 4 events (irreversible paraplegia or quadriplegia, 4 patients) and level 5 events (death, 4 patients) were mostly due to accidental antiseptic bolus administration. Inadvertent neuraxial drug administration occurred at different locations and during various stages of clinical care. The Human Factors Analysis Classification System (HFACS) identified unsafe acts related to skill-based errors and misidentification of routinely used objects. Additional deficiencies included organisational processes, resources, supervision, and task execution for neuraxial anaesthesia or analgesia. CONCLUSIONS: Level 4 and 5 harm was mainly associated with the administration of antiseptic solutions. The HFACS framework-based analysis suggested multiple modifiable institutional and individual deficiencies. Multidisciplinary improvements of organisational safety procedures, relevant preconditions, and neuraxial clinical practices may help prevent these serious incidents.

items.title: No Trace, No Claim: Two Contracts for Database Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents can generate database operations and explain their results, but current interfaces often leave a gap between generated plans, execution conditions, and claims presented to users. We argue that agent-facing data systems need two enforceable contracts. A plan contract defines what an agent may execute and reference; an evidence contract records the belief state, completeness, and provenance under which a result supports a claim. We instantiate these contracts in TGMS, a bi-temporal graph system in which an LLM plans over a fixed temporal operator interface. A static verifier checks plans before execution, and a claim verifier checks typed claims against content-addressed traces. Live model runs exposed two failures missed by input-only schemas and value-only grounding: nonexistent result fields and page-local counts reported as complete-result counts. Result-field checking makes the first a repairable rejection. Completeness propagation detects the second in all 15 controlled cases and misses all 15 when disabled. On the frozen CollegeMsg workload, TGMS reaches 0.408 typed-answer accuracy versus 0.064--0.284 for the evaluated baselines. On Bitcoin-OTC, direct SQL over the same bi-temporal store matches TGMS, showing no universal accuracy advantage for the fixed operator interface. On correction probes, TGMS and bi-temporal SQL answer historical-belief questions, while latest-state baselines cannot. Before claim gating, 21 of 220 answers contain an unsupported gated claim; after gating, none of 199 emitted answers does, at the cost of 21 fewer answers. The plan contract makes invalid plans rejectable and execution reproducible under recorded conditions, while the evidence contract makes gated claims faithful to cited evidence. Neither guarantees correct interpretation of user intent.

items.title: Nobody Truly Agrees on Sentiment: Humans, Bespoke Tools, and LLMs Struggle with Social Media Texts
items.abstract: Social media is a rich source of real-time public sentiment, but widely used sentiment analysis tools are often applied without understanding their limitations. In this study, we evaluate the inter-rater reliability of three bespoke sentiment analysis tools (TextBlob, VADER, and Twitter-roBERTa-base) and three large language models (LLMs: Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama-4-Maverick-17B) against six human raters across 100 tweets. We measured agreement using two statistical measures: Cohen's kappa for pairwise comparisons and Fleiss' kappa for multiple raters. Even among the human raters, our results showed only fair agreement, highlighting the subjectivity of sentiment analysis. Higher agreement was observed under the binary sentiment classification (negative vs. non-negative and positive vs. non-positive) than under the three-class classification across both humans and automated tools. The Twitter-roBERTa-base model showed the strongest alignment with human ratings, outperforming both bespoke sentiment tools and LLMs, particularly in distinguishing negative versus non-negative sentiment. LLMs showed substantial agreement among themselves and moderate to substantial alignment with humans, performing better in positive vs. non-positive classifications. Our findings underscore that domain-specific fine-tuning remains crucial for reliable social media sentiment analysis, and human-centered evaluation remains essential for establishing gold-standard labels.

items.title: Nursing under pressure: identity, challenges and coping during pandemic a qualitative study
items.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound impact on the lives of nurses. The increased workload, heightened risk of infection, and experiences of social isolation have significantly affected their physical and psychological well-being. Despite these challenges, nurses have continued to perform their duties with unwavering dedication, playing a pivotal role in the fight against the pandemic. This study aims to explore how nurses’ coping strategies and occupational experiences were shaped by the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. A phenomenological research design, one of the qualitative research methods, was employed in this study. The research was conducted with eight nurses who actively provided care to COVID-19 patients and voluntarily agreed to participate. The participants were aged between 26 and 43 years; all were female, and two were single. Data were collected using a demographic information form and a semi-structured interview form, and analyzed through phenomenological analysis. Four main themes emerged from the analysis: (1) Professional Identity and Changes in the Work Environment (2), Embodied Consequences (3), Moral Distress and Existential Dilemmas, and (4) Resilience in Adversity. The findings indicate that the pandemic increased nurses’ workload, negatively impacted their physical and psychological health, and led to challenges such as social isolation. Nurses relied on peer support, psychological assistance, and personal coping strategies to navigate these difficulties. The COVID-19 pandemic had a profound and multidimensional impact on nurses’ professional and social lives. To safeguard the physical, psychological, and social well-being of nurses during crises such as pandemics, it is crucial to promote effective coping strategies, ensure access to ergonomic equipment, and strengthen professional support mechanisms. This study contributes to understanding nurses’ experiences during the pandemic and to enhancing preparedness for future crises.

items.title: Obstacles to the Development of Creative Competence and Evidence-based Strategies for Overcoming Them among Higher Education Students
items.abstract: The development of creative competence has become a strategic priority in contemporary higher education, driven by thegrowing demand for innovation, adaptability, critical thinking, and eff ective problem-solving in rapidly changing professionalenvironments. In the context of globalization, digital transformation, and knowledge-based economies, creative competence isincreasingly recognized as a core component of transversal competences that determine graduates’ competitiveness,employability, and capacity for lifelong learning. Despite its signifi cance, however, many higher education institutions stillstruggle to create conditions conducive to the systematic and sustainable development of students’ creativity. The purpose ofthis article is to identify and analyze the key obstacles to the development of creative competence among higher educationstudents and to propose and justify evidence-based strategies for overcoming these challenges. The research is grounded in amixed-methods approach, integrating a critical review of contemporary scholarly literature with empirical data obtainedthrough surveys and semi-structured interviews conducted among students and academic staff . The fi ndings suggest that thebarriers to creative competence development are complex, multifaceted, and interrelated. Institutional factors include rigidcurricula, limited academic autonomy, and insuffi cient support for innovative teaching practices. Pedagogical challenges areassociated with the dominance of traditional, teacher-centered methods that prioritize memorization and standardized outcomesover creativity and independent thinking. Psychological barriers such as fear of making mistakes, low intrinsic motivation,anxiety, and lack of self-effi cacy further constrain students’ creative expression. Additionally, socio-cultural factors and assessment systems that undervalue originality contribute to the persistence of the problem. Creating a supportive, inclusive,and student-centered learning environment is also identifi ed as a crucial condition for fostering creativity. The results of theresearch contribute to the theoretical advancement of the concept of creative competence in higher education and providepractical recommendations for educators, curriculum developers, and policymakers aimed at improving the quality andrelevance of higher education in the modern world.

items.title: Occupational violence in patient safety and quality of care: a scoping review protocol
items.abstract: Workplace violence (WPV) is a significant issue that negatively affects job satisfaction, compromising the physical and mental health of healthcare workers, impacting the care provided and the organizational climate, and causing harm related to the safety and quality of patient care. WPV can manifest itself both among healthcare team members and in interactions between workers, patients, visitors, and companions. This study aims to describe the planning of a scoping review that will map the evidence on the consequences of workplace violence against healthcare workers regarding patient safety and quality of care. This is a scoping review protocol that follows the methodological guidelines designated by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the recommendations for drafting scoping reviews of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols - extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). It will follow the subsequent steps: definition and alignment of the objective and research question, eligibility criteria, description of the planned approach for the search, selection, extraction, analysis, and presentation of evidence, and the formulation of conclusions and implications of the findings. By systematizing the existing knowledge, this protocol may support scientific advancement at the interface between occupational health and patient safety, reinforcing the need to integrate such dimensions in healthcare practice, management, and research, aiming at the qualification of care and the protection of workers and patients.

items.abstract: Sickness certification is a common and demanding task in Swedish primary care, particularly for patients with mental health conditions, for whom assessments of work ability and functional impairment are often associated with considerable uncertainty. Drawing on the findings of Falk et al., the authors argue that longer or more detailed sickness certificates do not improve the consistency or quality of physicians' assessments but do increase the administrative burden. The authors advocate shifting the focus from documentation towards active rehabilitation. Suggested strategies include earlier access to evidence-based treatment, greater use of part-time sickness absence, stronger workplace involvement, and closer collaboration among healthcare services,occupational health services, employers, the Social Insurance Agency, and the Public Employment Service. Behavioural medicine approaches may also help strengthen patients' problem-solving skills and reduce the risk of prolonged dependence on sickness absence.

items.title: Omni-Diffusion-Distill: Few-Step Distillation of Unified Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
items.abstract: Unified multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) offer a single architecture for both image generation and multimodal understanding, but their iterative decoding requires tens to hundreds of forward passes. Existing few-step distillation methods largely focus on either image generation or text generation, making it unclear how to compress a fully discrete multimodal dLLM into a single efficient student while preserving both generation and understanding. We introduce Omni-Diffusion-Distill, a unified two-stage distillation framework that retains strong generation and understanding capabilities while substantially reducing the inference cost of a unified multimodal dLLM. Omni-Diffusion-Distill aligns the distillation of both generation and understanding, for both images and text, in the discrete token space. In the first stage, the student is trained to skip decoding steps by replaying cached teacher trajectories, and in the second stage the student is refined on intermediate states along its own rollouts. We further remedy two sources of degradation in unified distillation with a pairwise collision penalty that reduces repetition under parallel text decoding, and entropy-matched guidance that prevents entropy collapse caused by fitting the sharpened teacher distribution in image generation. Omni-Diffusion-Distill achieves state-of-the-art trade-offs between decoding efficiency and generation and understanding performance for multimodal dLLMs, reducing image generation from 128 to 8 decoding steps and multimodal understanding from 512 to 64, giving 18.2x and 21.2x wall-clock speedups. Under these budgets, it scores 0.828 on GenEval and 83.0 on DPG-Bench for text-to-image generation, while reaching GPT judge scores of 20.0 on MM-Vet and 57.2 on COCO captioning (twice the teacher's 28.4 at the same steps) for multimodal understanding.

items.title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents
items.abstract: We study whether small LLM agents can operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets by both respecting the allocated runtime and using available time productively. We evaluate Qwen3.6-27B on five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Qwen3-4B on Zork I (Jericho), two agentic benchmarks where additional computational time can meaningfully improve performance. In the simplest setting, where the budget is stated only in the prompt, agents fail to translate the stated budget into controlled use of time. These failures arise from gaps in time awareness, since the harness provides no timing feedback, but also because they cannot reliably anticipate the duration of actions, and do not have a learned mapping from available time to an appropriate strategy. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based mechanisms that expose timing information and enforce deadlines, and reinforcement learning with budget-aware rewards. Injecting timing information through the harness substantially improves budget adherence for Qwen3.6-27B without measurable loss in performance, while enforcement hooks tighten adherence further. RL with GRPO achieves near-perfect budget adherence on Zork I and generalizes to held-out budgets not seen during training, but does not improve task performance over the untrained harness on MLE-Bench. Once agents are made to respect the budget, they still fail to use additional time to improve task performance. RL-trained policies learn when to stop but often fill extra time with repeated actions, and GRPO training on multiple budgets tends to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget. Our results reveal a gap between time adherence and productive time allocation, which remains a central challenge for budget-conditioned agents.

items.title: On-Demand Robotic Assembly via Differentiable Geometric Part Repair
items.abstract: Transitioning from a digital design to a robotic assembly process currently requires months of expert manual tuning to reconcile part geometries with robotic constraints. This paper presents an end-to-end, autonomous pipeline for the design and physical construction of bespoke wooden assemblies. A generative AI agent translates user prompts into initial 3D geometries, balancing the visual fidelity of the design with select physical constraints. The assemblability of the design is further improved by a gradient-based repair stage that backpropagates through a graph attention network surrogate to adjust component geometries. In addition to correcting for disjointed and overlapping components, we demonstrate hardware-specific corrections, differentiably optimizing the geometry of components to enable robot screwdriving for 86.7% of 60 novel natural language inputs, significantly outperforming prior work by a factor of ten. For ten of the structures, we physically demonstrate assemblability with two UR5e robots. This work marks a meaningful step toward on-demand robotic manufacturing, enabling the rapid production of customized, low-volume goods.
